newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Analysts predict trouble if Russian army not paid.
newsitem.headline: Analysts predict trouble if Russian army not paid.

text.p: Security chief Alexander Lebed may have gone over the top on Wednesday in predicting an imminent mutiny in Russia's armed forces but analysts said there would be trouble if soldiers did not get paid soon.
Lebed's apocalyptic warning came amid a flood of media reports about the parlous state of the armed forces, including plummeting morale, hunger and a dramatic increase in suicides.
In a sign of government concern, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin met top generals on Wednesday to discuss funding problems in the army, where wages have gone unpaid for months.
"An armed mutiny may take place this autumn," Lebed, a chisel-jawed former general, told Vechernyaya Moskva newspaper.
In the few months since he was appointed President Boris Yeltsin's national security adviser, Lebed has won a reputation for a dramatic turn of phrase and a talent for self promotion.

But analysts said that in this case he had good reason to raise the alarm. "It's not a political game. It's a result of the catastrophic situation in the armed forces," said Alexander Goltz, leading commentator of the army daily Krasnaya Zvezda.
His paper said on Wednesday that 123 soldiers had killed themselves so far this year, 28 percent more than last year, and said poverty and hopelessness were largely to blame.
Senior lieutenant Yuri Khoruzhev shot himself because he could not feed his family. His unit had no money for the funeral and his coffin was secured on the word of a senior officer.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov has said he too goes without pay and that many soldiers are turning to crime to survive.
"The army is a kind of body where people are used to living from wage to wage...If there is no money, what are they supposed to do?" he said in remarks to the Komsomolskaya Pravda daily.
"So they become involved in all kinds of illegal activities, commercial structures and they join criminals, so to speak. And we are talking here about people with weapons in their hands."
Alexander Konovalov, military analyst at U.S.A. and Canada Institute, said the lack of funds had forced the army to "privatise" -- sell off weapons and equipment on a grand scale.
Apart from dramatically reducing the army's capacity to fight -- as shown during 21 months of futile and bloody conflict in Chechnya -- the sell-offs hold more immediate dangers.
Several soldiers were blown up when a missile exploded in the Far East this month -- reports said the soldiers had been trying to strip down the warhead to sell for scrap.

Lebed accused the government of burying its head in the sand and compared the situation to 1916 when the Russian army, demoralised in World War One, began to split and was in no position to stop the Bolshevik revolution the following year.

Goltz disputed the comparison, saying today's communist opposition appeared unable to turn the army against the government as Lenin had done. But he did not rule out spontaneous protests among soldiers and officers.
Konovalov took a similar line. "There's no prospect of an uprising in a single, organised body. But rather an increase in the number of guns being sold, low morale, poor discipline."

Soldiers, who have been seen begging for food on the streets, are not the only ones to feel the squeeze. Labour Minister Gennady Melikyan said on Wednesday that over a third of salaries were not being paid and the debt was growing.
With this year's money running out and next year's budget in the works, every interest group is screaming, although the military's calls clearly have a steel edge.
Konavlyov said the only answer was to adapt Russia's armed forces to the post Cold-War era and its economic capacities.

But he said former defence minister Pavel Grachev did not implement reforms, which include cutting the army from two million to 1.5 million. "Under Grachev the only army reform was to change the red star for the double-headed eagle."

Rodionov, who took over in July, has not had time to make his mark, but he had a warning for any who try to ignore the problem. "People go mad sometimes...Who can guarantee that in such circumstances one can expect good? On the contrary, one can expect anything to happen."
